video.title: The Simplest Business in a Box Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mark, a 66-year-old lawyer who designs 'business in a box' ideas, about his nitro iced coffee cart built from a gutted Home Depot tool cart for under ~$1-3k. Using shelf-stable brewed coffee in bag-in-box packs and a nitro tap, he pours 24oz iced coffees in 30 seconds for ~$3 cost and ~$8.50 price, netting $400 at small events, $800-1,200 at festivals and $8,000 at his best two-day event. He also ran beer tap trucks and armoire tap bar rentals, and sets up operators (divorced moms, veterans, visa immigrants) on a ~30% profit split. Key takeaway: strip a product to what customers actually buy, keep capex tiny, and win on location.

speakers.name: Mark
speakers.description: Lawyer and serial small-business builder; founder of Sunburst Nitro Coffee carts

ideas.name: Nitro iced coffee cart at events and high-traffic locations
ideas.one_liner: Serve pre-brewed nitro iced coffee from a gutted Home Depot tool cart with a tap, selling 24oz cups at events, fairs, car shows, farmers markets and car washes.
ideas.customer: Attendees of fairs, festivals, air shows, cars-and-coffee, night markets, farmers markets, car wash customers
ideas.problem: Coffee trucks need $30k espresso machines and take minutes per cup; most drinks after 9am are iced with syrup so bean quality matters little
ideas.offer: Iced coffee/latte with cream and syrup poured in 30 seconds from bag-in-box brewed coffee and a nitro tap

pricing.notes: Unit cost ~$3 (coffee ~$1.50, cup ~$0.30, ice, sales tax). Venue/booth fees $150-500; one big event fee $300-400.

acquisition_channels.details: Books fairs, festivals, air shows, night markets, cars-and-coffee, Tractor Supply parking lots and car washes; relationships with event organisers; prefers meeting venue owners via LinkedIn/conferences ('side door').

quote.text: I get there early so that I can look and see how they're setting up, see where the traffic is coming in
quote.speaker: Mark

ideas.delivery: Owner or operator wheels cart to the venue; brewed coffee from a local supplier in bag-in-box; nitrogen tank refilled every ~2 months; FedEx Office PVC signs.
unit_economics_claims: Costs ~$3 per cup, sells for ~$8.50, ~$5 profit
Best event: $8,000 net over two hot days
ideas.startup_cost: Under $1,000 to about $2,500-3,000 (cart $600, tap $200, nitro tank a couple hundred, plus build labour ~$500)

acquisition.how: Event bookings and venue deals are manual relationships.

uk_applicability.notes: UK: street trading licence from the council, food business registration and hygiene rating, mobile trader insurance; event pitch fees; iced coffee demand is more seasonal in UK weather; card-only payments common.

risks: Permits for street vending ('cowboying' without permits)
Signage confusion about what you sell

tactics.name: Strip the coffee cart down to what customers buy
steps: Observe that after 9am most drinks are iced with syrup/cream
Skip $30k espresso machines; buy brewed coffee from a local brewer
Switch from heavy kegs to bag-in-box with a gas-driven pump
Limit menu to iced coffee and latte with a few syrups
Pour in 30 seconds

quote.text: the second you put that cream and that syrup in there, the quality of the underlying coffee doesn't matter
quote.speaker: Mark

tactics.name: Event pitch selection and placement
steps: Arrive early to watch set-up and traffic flow
Prefer the food area over isolated merchandise areas
Pick events without competing options (air shows, remote festivals)
Calibrate: bad days usually mean wrong location, date or season

quote.text: I believe that I'm better off in the food area
quote.speaker: Mark

tactics.name: Cheap, testable signage
steps: Design signs on your computer
Print on PVC at FedEx Office for ~$100
Iterate wording; simple 'ICE COFFEE' outperformed 'nitro' and 'latte'

quote.text: I now go back to just ice coffee. That's it
quote.speaker: Mark

tactics.name: Become the organiser's helper to get into events
steps: Support a new event organiser early (lend trucks, fill gaps)
Earn favourable access and fees as they grow

tactics.name: Card-only revenue split for operators
steps: Set operators up on your Stripe or Square account
Revenue lands in your account
Split ~30% to you depending on who supplies what

quote.text: They use my Stripe account, a Stripe account or a square account
quote.speaker: Mark

tactics.name: Side-door venue access
steps: Meet gas station/car wash owners on LinkedIn or at conferences
Pitch a story (e.g. a single mum operating 10-3) rather than asking about fees
Target car washes, gas stations, semi-pro sports, food courts

warnings.warning: Expensive equipment-heavy setups ($30k espresso machines, $50k trucks) kill returns and break down.

quote.text: get rid of that $30,000 coffee machine that breaks down and cost $5,000 to fix every time
quote.speaker: Mark

warnings.warning: Alcohol events bring liability worries (over-serving, underage drinking verdicts).
Wrong location, date or season can produce $100 days.
Operating without permits ('cowboying') is risky; public street vending is most regulated. UK note: street trading consents and food registration required.

quote.text: when I started it, I was cowboying it, not worrying about the permits
quote.speaker: Mark

warnings.warning: Founders romanticise product aspects customers don't care about.
Heavy kegs are a human-factors problem (injuries) and exclude many operators.

lessons.lesson: Sell what customers actually buy, not what the founder is romantic about.

quote.text: usually we're not romantic about the same things that our customers are romantic about. And that disconnect is very expensive
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Lower the cost of being wrong: a cheap, non-perishable setup makes testing locations cheap.

quote.text: the cost for being wrong is gas money and 150 bucks that you might have paid for that location
quote.speaker: Mark

lessons.lesson: Cluster with competitors: food courts and auto rows beat being the unique option.
A simple menu speeds service and increases throughput.
Design for human factors so more kinds of operators can run it.
Young founders with a working concept often give away territories cheaply; strike deals early.
Watch bankrupt businesses: owners who don't cut costs early go down.
Approach gatekeepers through the side door with a story, not a cold ask about fees.

quote.text: I don't believe in going in the front door because of the gate
quote.speaker: Mark

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with specific unit costs and event results, but a part-time hobby scale and a Whisper tiny transcript with mis-heard numbers (e.g. '$3,400, $500', '850').
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Sponsor reads for GoHighLevel; host promotes TK Owners.
